title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
statement: You get the root of a binary tree. Return how many levels it has: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree has depth 0.

example.caption: The longest way down is 3 -> 20 -> 15 (or 7). That is 3 nodes, so the depth is 3.

idea.sentence: The depth of a tree is 1 plus the deeper of its two subtrees, and an empty tree has depth 0.

jargon.plain: How many nodes are on the longest path from a node down to a leaf. A lone leaf is 1.

watch.inputHint: One argument: the tree as a level-order array, null for a missing child, e.g. [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]

compare.bruteLabel: Keep a queue of a whole level at once (level by level)
compare.optimalLabel: Recursion, only the current path on the stack
compare.unit: extra memory cells, for a balanced tree

rows.name: Level by level (BFS)
rows.note: Count how many levels you walk. The queue can hold a whole wide level.

rows.name: Recursion (DFS)
rows.note: Every node is visited once. The call stack holds one root-to-node path.

fast.takeaway: Every node must be looked at once, so time is O(n). Recursion only remembers one path at a time, which is the height.

stages.title: Empty spot
stages.note: No node means no levels. Return 0.

stages.title: Ask both sides
stages.note: Call the function on the left child and on the right child. Each call hands back its own depth.

stages.title: Add one level
stages.note: Take the deeper side and add 1 for this node. Return that to the parent.

edges.title: Empty tree
edges.why: The root is null. The empty case returns 0, not 1.

edges.title: Single node
edges.why: Two empty sides give 0 each. 1 + max(0, 0) = 1.

edges.title: Chain
edges.why: One side is always empty, so the depth is just the number of nodes.

edges.title: Deep on one side only
edges.why: Take the max of the two sides. Adding them would count two branches at once.

gotchas.text: Return 0 for an empty tree. Returning 1 there makes every depth off by one.
Use max of the two sides, not the sum and not the left side only. Only the deeper side decides the answer.
Math.max(left, right) is fine for two numbers. Do not spread a big array into Math.max: very long arrays overflow the argument limit.
The built-in max needs Go 1.21 or newer. On older versions write a tiny helper function.
A very tall, skinny tree makes recursion very deep. For millions of nodes use a level-by-level loop instead.

recap.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(h) call stack.
moves: Get the depth of the left and right sides
